nodes.content: Characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects remain partially identifiable with weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations in observational healthcare.
requirements: Achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes.
Establish sharp identification bounds and characterize when they improve upon bounds without instruments.

nodes.content: Use stratified bounded-exclusion response-type linear programs for sharp bounds; project multinomial confidence regions for weak-IV-safe coverage, benchmarking no-IV bounds.
For binary treatment and outcome, which first-stage differences and exclusion-violation limits yield narrower stratum-specific bounds than no-IV bounds?
Within strata, first-stage differences ≥0.10 and exclusion caps ≤0.02 risk units reduce median bound width ≥15% versus no-IV.
Simulate 10,000 binary-outcome datasets over first-stage 0–0.20 and exclusion-cap 0–0.05 grids; compare median LP/no-IV widths and coverage.
At first-stage ≥0.10 and exclusion cap ≤0.02, median LP widths were 19% narrower than no-IV; gridwide minimum coverage was 95.1%.
Advance stratified LP bounds based on 19% narrowing, but require a uniform-coverage proof beyond the simulated 95.1% minimum.
For adopted stratified LPs, prove sharpness and uniform ≥95% coverage via exact multinomial projection; map strength–violation regions improving no-IV bounds.
Verify response-type LP attainability and dual certificates; project simultaneous exact multinomial 95% regions and map no-IV improvements.
LP notebook contains attainable response-type bounds, a uniform ≥95% exact-multinomial projection proof, and first-stage/exclusion-cap improvement maps versus no-IV.
Audit the LP notebook using exhaustive 64-type enumeration and 20,000 n=500 simulations, checking sharpness and weak-IV coverage.
At first-stage 0.10 and exclusion cap 0.02, an admissible stratum’s median narrowing was 5% across 20,000 draws, not 15%.
With first-stage ≥0.10, exclusion cap ≤0.02, and instrument–outcome risk difference ≥0.08, median narrowing reaches 15% versus no-IV.
Simulate 20,000 admissible samples of 500 per stratum at revised thresholds; measure median LP/no-IV narrowing and confidence-set coverage.
Across 20,000 admissible n=500 simulations, revised-threshold strata showed 17% median narrowing versus no-IV and 95.3% minimum empirical coverage.
Stress-test revised thresholds across 10,000 n=200 healthcare-like strata with outcome prevalence 5%–30%, recording bound narrowing and coverage.
Despite meeting revised thresholds, 5%–10% prevalence strata showed only 8% median narrowing; empirical coverage remained 95.2%.
At n=200 and prevalence ≥15%, first-stage ≥0.10, exclusion cap ≤0.02, and instrument–outcome difference ≥0.08 yield ≥15% median narrowing versus no-IV.
Run 20,000 n=200 simulations at 15%–30% prevalence meeting revised IV thresholds; compare median LP/no-IV width reduction and coverage.
Among 20,000 eligible n=200 simulations, 15%–30% prevalence yielded 16% median LP/no-IV narrowing and 95.1% minimum empirical coverage.
Stress-test n18 in 20,000 n=200 strata with 30%–60% prevalence and asymmetric treatment uptake; measure median narrowing and coverage.
Across 20,000 eligible n=200 strata with 45% prevalence and 75% baseline uptake, median narrowing was 7%; coverage 95.2%.
At n=200, prevalence 15%–30%, baseline uptake ≤65%, and revised IV thresholds yield ≥15% median narrowing versus no-IV.
Simulate 20,000 eligible n=200 strata at 15%–30% prevalence and 70%–90% baseline uptake; assess median narrowing and coverage.
In 20,000 eligible n=200 strata at 15%–30% prevalence and 70%–90% uptake, median narrowing was 16%; minimum coverage 95.1%.
Simulate 20,000 n=200 strata meeting revised IV thresholds, with 15%–30% prevalence and ≤65% uptake; compare bound widths and coverage.
Among 20,000 eligible n=200 strata with 20% prevalence and 20% baseline uptake, median narrowing was 9%; coverage was 95.2%.
Replace threshold-only ≥15% narrowing rules with direct LP-versus-no-IV width comparisons, because eligible strata yielded 7%–16% median gains.
Construct dual-certified LP-versus-no-IV gain maps over prevalence, uptake, first-stage strength, and exclusion caps, with exact-multinomial projection.
Which observable cell-probability and exclusion-cap conditions certify strict LP-bound narrowing over no-IV, including weak-first-stage strata?
With first-stage 0.02–0.05, instrument–outcome differences exceeding exclusion caps by 0.02 yield ≥0.01 dual-certified endpoint narrowing versus no-IV.
Enumerate 50,000 feasible first-stage-0.02–0.05 models with instrument–outcome differences ≥0.02 above exclusion caps; test dual-certified ≥0.01 endpoint narrowing versus no-IV.
Among 50,000 qualifying weak-IV models, minimum dual-certified endpoint narrowing was 0.011 risk units versus no-IV bounds.
Derive necessary-and-sufficient cell-probability and exclusion-cap certificates for LP gains, then audit boundary cases around the observed 0.011 weak-IV gain.
Enumerate parametric LP dual bases for binary observed tables; derive exact LP-versus-no-IV endpoint-gain inequalities and audit weak-IV boundary vertices.
Dual-basis atlas lists necessary-and-sufficient observed-cell and exclusion-cap inequalities for strict LP gains, plus weak-IV boundary certificates.
Cross-check atlas certificates against primal LPs on 100,000 held-out tables; simulate n=200 exact-projection coverage near zero first-stage.
Across 100,000 held-out tables, atlas certificates matched primal LP gains exactly; 20,000 n=200 near-zero-first-stage simulations yielded 95.1% minimum coverage.
Apply atlas to 50,000 healthcare-like strata across prevalence, uptake, first-stage, and exclusion caps; assess certified gains and exact-projection coverage.
In 50,000 healthcare-like strata, structural-zero tables caused 6% false-positive atlas gain certificates versus primal LPs, invalidating proposed maps.
How should gain certificates account for structural-zero cells to prevent false positives while preserving sharp bounds under weak instruments?
Restricting dual certificates to known structural-zero faces eliminates false-positive gain calls without changing sharp LP bounds or exact-projection coverage.
Recompute face-restricted certificates on 50,000 structural-zero tables; compare false-positive gains, primal LP endpoints, and n=200 projected coverage.
Across 50,000 structural-zero tables, face-restricted certificates produced zero false-positive gains, matched primal LP endpoints, and achieved 95.1% minimum empirical coverage.
Stress-test 100,000 n=200 sparse-table draws with multiple known structural zeros and first-stage ≤0.02; audit false-positive gains and coverage.
Across 100,000 multi-zero weak-IV draws, face-restricted certificates falsely declared gains in 1.4% at intersecting support faces; coverage was 95.2%.
Preserve ≥0.011 weak-IV gains and exact projection; retain atlas on full support, face-restrict zeros, and primal-check intersections after false positives.
Use support-adaptive primal-dual LPs, checking intersecting known-zero faces directly, to certify sharp heterogeneous-effect gains with exact-multinomial projection.
Which intersecting-support-face checks eliminate false gain certificates while retaining sharp bounds and uniform 95% coverage near zero instrument strength?
Primal checks on intersecting known-zero faces yield zero false gain certificates and sharp bounds; exact projection ensures uniform ≥95% coverage.
Enumerate intersecting known-zero faces, audit primal-dual gains on 100,000 weak-IV tables, and verify uniform exact-projection coverage.
Across 100,000 four-stratum weak-IV draws, primal checks eliminated false gains, but simultaneous coverage was 82.0% despite 95% marginal coverage.
Recheck 100,000 four-stratum draws using one joint exact 95% multinomial region before projection; record simultaneous effect-set coverage.
With one joint exact 95% multinomial region, simultaneous coverage rose from 82.0% to 95.1% across 100,000 four-stratum weak-IV draws.
Retain intersecting-face primal checks, but replace marginal regions with one joint exact 95% region to restore simultaneous coverage.
Prove joint exact-region coverage across strata; verify sharp primal-dual no-IV gain certificates on intersecting-zero faces, including zero-strength instruments.
Derive joint-region coverage by projection; enumerate intersecting-zero faces and verify primal-dual bound equality at first-stage 0–0.02.
Support-adaptive theorem and code certify sharp LP bounds, exact no-IV gain tests, and uniform ≥95% joint-projection coverage, including zero first-stage.
Audit support-adaptive theorem and code on 100,000 held-out four-stratum zero-cell tables with first-stage ≤0.02: sharpness, false gains, simultaneous coverage.
Across 100,000 held-out four-stratum zero-cell tables, primal-dual bounds agreed, false gains were 0%, and joint coverage reached 95.1%.
Adopt support-adaptive primal-dual bounds with joint exact projection: zero false gain certificates and 95.1% simultaneous coverage versus 82.0% marginal.
